pedagogy.summary: This is a PROCEDURAL topic: the skill of representing the solar system to SCALE and interpreting such models, with one headline discovery — the distances between planets are vastly larger than the planets themselves, so much so that you cannot show true planet SIZES and true DISTANCES on the same easy scale. The canonical demonstration: if the Sun were a beach ball, Earth would be a pea tens of metres away; a size-and-distance model to a single scale has to be spread over half a mile or more. Children learn to choose a scale, use proportional reasoning to place objects, and read what a scale model is (and isn't) telling them — confronting the crowded-together picture they get from textbook diagrams.
bestPractices: Make the size-vs-distance tension the core lesson: build (or examine) a size model AND a distance model and discover you can't do both on one convenient scale — a true combined model needs a huge space (JPL: at least half a mile).

Ground it in proportional reasoning: pick a scale (e.g. Sun = a ball of size X), then use the same ratio to work out every planet's size and distance — connecting to the maths of ratio/scaling the child is meeting.
Use an embodied, physical build where possible — pace out a distance model across a field or corridor with beads/markers — so the enormous empty gaps are FELT with the body, not just seen on a page.

Confront the textbook-diagram misconception explicitly: the neat lined-up-planets image is NOT to scale for distance (and often not for size) — real space is mostly emptiness; use the model to correct it.
Keep the numbers meaningful, not overwhelming: a couple of anchor facts (Sun-as-beach-ball → Earth-as-pea ~26 m; Neptune billions of km out) do more than a full table of figures at this age.
keyRepresentations: Beach-ball Sun / pea Earth ~26 m away — the anchor scale comparison
Two separate models: a SIZE model (planets shrunk in proportion) and a DISTANCE model (spacing shrunk in proportion), shown to be incompatible on one scale
A scale ratio / proportion tool: Scale size ÷ real size = Scale distance ÷ real distance
A 'toilet-paper' / bead-on-a-string distance model pacing planets out along a line
A to-scale strip the child must scroll a long way across to travel from the Sun to the outer planets
commonMisconceptions: Thinking the planets are close together and the solar system is crowded (from textbook diagrams), rather than mostly vast empty space.
Assuming a single scale model can show both true planet sizes and true distances easily — missing that a same-scale model needs an enormous area.
Reading the common 'planets in a neat row, evenly spaced' picture as accurate for size and distance.
Confusing scaling SIZE with scaling DISTANCE — shrinking planets and gaps by different unstated amounts and not noticing.
Believing the outer planets are only a little farther than the inner ones, underestimating how distances balloon toward Neptune.
Thinking a scale model preserves everything (colours, moons, orbits precisely) rather than deliberately representing chosen quantities to a chosen ratio.

learn.summary: A procedural topic: children learn to build and interpret a scale model of the solar system, choosing a scale and applying the same proportion to every planet's size and distance. The headline discovery is that distances between planets are vastly larger than the planets themselves — so large that true sizes and true distances cannot both be shown easily on one convenient scale. The anchor comparison: if the Sun is a beach ball about 30 cm across, Earth is a peppercorn-sized bead (about 3 mm) roughly 32 metres away (about 30 m), and Neptune is about 30 times farther, nearly a kilometre away. The work confronts the textbook image of neatly lined-up, close-together planets, which is not to scale for distance (and often not for size).

activities.title: Pace out a scale solar system (whole-body distance model)
feedback: If a learner clusters the planets a few steps from the Sun (matching the textbook image), have them re-measure Earth's distance on the agreed scale and physically walk it so the empty gap is felt, then name the textbook picture as not-to-scale.

If a learner sizes the ball and Earth-bead correctly but squashes the distances (or stretches distances while over-sizing the planets), remind them a scale model uses ONE ruler for both — re-measure sizes and distances with the same scale factor and check they match.
If a learner places planets nearly touching, with gaps about the size of the planets, point out the real gaps are thousands of times the planet sizes — the solar system is overwhelmingly empty.
Prompt reflection: 'Roughly how many Earth-beads would fit end-to-end in the gap to the Sun?' (about 11,700) and 'Where does Neptune end up — still on the playground, or well past it?'
activities.rationale: The topic is procedural and spatial; an embodied build where the vast gaps are felt in the legs, not just seen on a page, makes the size-vs-distance contrast concrete and directly targets the crowded-together misconception. Building to one consistent ratio enacts the proportional-reasoning core.
sourceClaims: Distances in the solar system are so large (Sun to Neptune ~4 billion km) that a scale model showing planet SIZES and DISTANCES at the same scale must be spread over at least half a mile; models therefore usually show size OR distance, not both, and a 1-cm Earth puts Neptune about two miles away.

The common 'planets lined up in a neat row' image is not physically realistic and is used only to convey relative scale; building a scale model uses proportional reasoning (scale diameter/scale distance = actual diameter/actual distance).
learnerActions: Agree a scale with a concrete anchor: the Sun is a beach ball about 30 cm across; on the same scale Earth is a peppercorn-sized bead about 3 mm across (smaller than a pea).

Using a long tape measure and the run of a field, corridor, or playground, place the Earth-bead at the correct distance on this scale — for a ~30 cm ball this works out to about 32 metres (roughly 30 metres).
Walk out to where each further planet belongs, placing a bead or marker, and keep walking to where Neptune would stand — roughly 30 times farther than Earth, likely off the end of the playground.
Keep the SAME scale for both sizes and distances throughout; measure, don't guess.
Afterwards, compare what you paced out with a textbook 'planets in a neat row' picture and decide whether that picture is to scale.
activities.intendedInsight: The planets are tiny specks separated by huge, mostly empty gaps; the distances dwarf the planet sizes, and one consistent scale forces you to spread the model over a very large space.

activities.title: Choose a scale and apply the proportion
feedback: If sizes and distances are scaled by different unstated amounts, flag that both must share one ratio and have the learner recompute.

If a learner expects one tidy model to show everything, have them compute the combined length and see why it must be spread very far — e.g. an auto-note 'to show both, this model would be about N km long'.
Affirm when the learner correctly transfers the ratio to a new anchor (e.g. 'if the Sun were twice as big, every scaled distance doubles, so Earth moves twice as far out').
activities.rationale: Proportional reasoning is the mathematical heart of the skill; letting learners choose the scale and apply one ratio connects to the ratio/scaling maths they meet at this age and makes the size-vs-distance incompatibility arise from their own calculation rather than being asserted.
sourceClaims: Distances in the solar system are so large (Sun to Neptune ~4 billion km) that a scale model showing planet SIZES and DISTANCES at the same scale must be spread over at least half a mile; models therefore usually show size OR distance, not both, and a 1-cm Earth puts Neptune about two miles away.

The common 'planets lined up in a neat row' image is not physically realistic and is used only to convey relative scale; building a scale model uses proportional reasoning (scale diameter/scale distance = actual diameter/actual distance).
learnerActions: Pick the Sun's model size (e.g. a ball of a chosen diameter) as the scale anchor.
Use the proportion scale size ÷ real size = scale distance ÷ real distance to work out each planet's scaled size and scaled distance from the same ratio.
Build (or set up on a build-and-scroll tool) a SIZE model and a separate DISTANCE model, and try to combine them on one scale.
Record how long the combined model would have to be for both to be shown together.
Check your anchor facts: a 30 cm beach-ball Sun gives a peppercorn-sized Earth (about 3 mm) roughly 32 metres away; Neptune, about 4.5 billion km out, lands about 30 times farther (nearly 1 km).
activities.intendedInsight: A single scale applied consistently to sizes and distances cannot show both comfortably on one convenient layout — a true combined model needs an enormous space (e.g. with a 1-cm Earth, the Sun is about 1.1 m across and Neptune is about 3.5 km, over two miles, away; the length depends on the scale chosen). You choose which quantity a model represents.

activities.title: Travel the gaps on screen (digital build-and-scroll or flight)
feedback: When a learner is surprised by how long they must scroll/fly to reach Neptune, name it: 'the space between planets is enormous compared with the planets.'

Use the banner/readout ('to show size AND distance together, this model would be about N metres long — nearly a kilometre for a 30 cm Sun, and longer for a bigger Sun') to confirm the incompatibility the learner just experienced.
If the learner treats the textbook row as accurate, prompt the to-scale comparison strip.
activities.rationale: A build-and-scroll tool supports the procedural core (choose scale → apply proportion → interpret) and lets the learner traverse the gaps; a true-scale 3D flight is powerful for feeling that distance dwarfs size. Both are screen stand-ins for the bodily pacing experience and hint at, rather than reproduce, whole-body scale.
sourceClaims: Distances in the solar system are so large (Sun to Neptune ~4 billion km) that a scale model showing planet SIZES and DISTANCES at the same scale must be spread over at least half a mile; models therefore usually show size OR distance, not both, and a 1-cm Earth puts Neptune about two miles away.
learnerActions: On a build-your-own-scale-model tool, set the Sun's size and let the tool place all planets to that scale.
Flip between a SIZE-scale view and a DISTANCE-scale view and note why they can't coexist comfortably on one page.
Pan or scroll to 'travel' from the Sun outward — past mostly empty black — to reach Earth, then keep going to Neptune; use a distance/time or length readout to register the emptiness.
Apply a 'is this to scale?' check to the neat lined-up textbook row and mark whether it is accurate for distance and size.
activities.intendedInsight: Even on screen, traversing the gaps shows the planets are tiny and the space between them is enormous; the lined-up textbook picture is not to scale.

activities.title: Check and read scale models (interpretation practice)
feedback: If a learner says a diagram is 'to scale' without checking, ask them to compare a planet size with the gap beside it on that diagram.
If a learner thinks a model preserves everything, clarify that a scale model deliberately represents chosen quantities to a chosen ratio.
Reinforce correct ordering and the fact that outer-planet distances balloon far beyond the inner ones.
activities.rationale: Interpretation and checking are part of the stated objective (create OR interpret). A static or quiz-style check can assess reasoning about size-vs-distance and ordering; it does not itself have the learner choose a scale, apply the ratio, or feel the distances, so it works best alongside a build or pacing activity.
sourceClaims: The common 'planets lined up in a neat row' image is not physically realistic and is used only to convey relative scale; building a scale model uses proportional reasoning (scale diameter/scale distance = actual diameter/actual distance).
learnerActions: Given a labelled scale diagram, tap or look up the scaled size and distance of each planet and state the anchor facts (30 cm beach-ball Sun → peppercorn-sized Earth, about 3 mm, roughly 32 m away).
Compare which is bigger: a planet, or the gap to the next planet.
Decide whether a given diagram is to scale for size, for distance, for both, or for neither, and justify your answer.
Sequence the planets by distance and estimate, e.g. where Earth sits if the Sun were a beach ball.
Explain what a scale model does and does not preserve (it shows chosen quantities to a chosen ratio, not necessarily colours, moons, or exact orbits).
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a scale model means knowing what quantity it represents and at what ratio — and that most diagrams compress distance to fit a page.

constraints: Keep the numbers meaningful, not overwhelming: a couple of anchor facts (a 30 cm beach-ball Sun → a peppercorn-sized Earth about 3 mm across, roughly 32 m away; Neptune about 4.5 billion km out, about 30 times farther than Earth) do more at this age than a full table of figures.

A whole-body pacing activity is the richest version because the vast emptiness is felt physically; screen build-and-scroll and 3D-flight tools convey the proportional reasoning and let learners traverse the gaps but only hint at the bodily scale shock — present them as approximations, not equivalents.

A static labelled diagram and a quiz/slider can present anchor facts and assess interpretation and ordering, but they do not let the learner choose a scale, apply the ratio independently, or build the model; use them to check understanding, not as the sole teaching of the procedural skill.

In-role dialogue can describe scale, reasoning, and anchor facts and can prompt discussion, but it does not itself let a learner build a model, apply the ratio, or feel the distances; treat it as a discussion support, not a substitute for a build or pacing activity.

A scale model represents chosen quantities (size or distance) to one chosen ratio; the same ratio must be used throughout, and a combined size-and-distance model requires an enormous space rather than a single convenient layout.

Anchor figures (about 32 m for Earth, which is about 3 mm across, under a ~30 cm beach-ball Sun; Neptune ~30 times farther, nearly 1 km) are approximate; compute exact placements from the proportion before relying on them for a precise build.
Watch what learners DO (where they physically place or set the planets), not only what they say, to reveal whether they hold one consistent scale.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: the source states a 1-cm Earth puts Neptune about two miles away; with the beach-ball (~30 cm Sun) anchor the material gives Earth-pea roughly 30 m and Neptune 'roughly 30 times farther' (hundreds of metres to ~1 km). These are different scales and both are internally consistent; retained as given but the two anchors should not be conflated.

Self-audit: a ~30 cm Sun scales Earth to nearer ~32 m; the learner-facing figures have been aligned to 'roughly 30 metres (about 32 m)' with ~26 m kept as the familiar rounded anchor. Treat all such figures as approximate and confirm exact placement from a proper scale calculation before classroom use.

The original row contained universal-style claims that in-role dialogue 'cannot let the child do or feel it' and that a static image 'can't let the child choose a scale'; these have been softened to scope-limited notes about what each format does and does not do, rather than asserted as universal pedagogical laws.

The original catalog gap and recommendation framed the digital build tool as 'the best available' stand-in; retained as an approximation note rather than as evidence of comparative efficacy, which the sources do not establish.

probeDeeper: On your model, roughly how many Earth-peas would fit end-to-end in the gap between the Earth and the Sun?
If I made the Sun twice as big, what would that do to where you place the Earth?
Where does Neptune end up — still on the playground, or well past it?
Why do you think textbook pictures show the planets close together if the real gaps are this enormous?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance applies one consistent scale: with the Sun as a ~30 cm beach ball, the Earth-pea is placed about 25–30 metres away, and Neptune ends up roughly 30 times farther still — hundreds of metres away, likely off the end of the playground. The child treats the planets as tiny specks separated by huge, mostly empty gaps, and does NOT shrink the distances to keep the planets near the Sun. The size-scale and the distance-scale stay the same throughout.

errorPatterns.pattern: makes the planets big and close together, like the textbook picture ('they all fit near the Sun')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Physically pace out the true scaled distances so the vast empty gaps are FELT; contrast with the compressed textbook image and name it as not-to-scale.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child clusters the planets a few steps from the Sun, hugely under-scaling the distances to match familiar diagrams

errorPatterns.pattern: uses one scale for the sizes and a different one for the distances
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: remind them a scale model must use ONE ruler for both — measure sizes and distances with the same scale factor and check they match.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child scales the ball and pea correctly but squashes the distances (or stretches distances while over-sizing the planets)

errorPatterns.pattern: places the planets nearly touching — gaps about the same as the planet sizes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the real gaps are thousands of times the planet sizes — the solar system is overwhelmingly empty space.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child sets the planets edge-to-edge or with gaps similar to the planets' own sizes

responseLevels.gap: Places the planets in a cluster near the Sun and/or sizes them inconsistently — distances squashed to fit a familiar diagram.
responseLevels.full: Builds or interprets a single consistent scale — tiny planets placed tens to hundreds of metres apart, Neptune off the field — and articulates that the gaps dwarf the planet sizes, transferring the scale factor to a new object.
responseLevels.partial: Applies the scale to EITHER sizes OR distances correctly but not both together (tiny planets bunched close, or right distances with oversized planets); says distances exceed sizes but the model doesn't show it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a working scale: the Sun is a beach ball about 30 cm across. Hand them a pea for Earth, a small bead for Neptune, a long tape measure, and the run of the playground. Set the task: 'Place the Earth-pea at the right distance from the Sun on THIS scale, then go and stand where Neptune would be.' Watch what they DO — do they keep the SAME scale for sizes and distances, and do they end up walking tens of metres out for Earth (and far off the playground for Neptune), rather than bunching the planets a few steps from the Sun?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who can only hold one scale places the planets a few steps apart (distances squashed to match the familiar textbook diagram) while sizing them roughly right — or blows the sizes up. A child who genuinely grasps solar-system scale walks the pea tens of metres out and realises Neptune is off the field, keeping size and distance on the SAME scale. Watching WHERE they physically place the planets — not what they say — reveals which, so this is set and watched, never asked about.
